Question: What is the selection process of the UPSC selection post recruitment?
Answer: Step 1: Scrutiny of the application is done by the UPSC to see if you meet the eligibility criteria (both education and/or experience) Step 2: A list of shortlisted candidates is published on the UPSC website and a chance is given to the un-shortlisted candidates to make representations if they think they should have been included. They can write and email to the UPSC. Step 3: The UPSC can hold a written examination for the post depending on the number of candidates. The written test is always followed by an interview. Else, there is only an interview. Step 4: UPSC conducts the interview at UPSC Bhawan, New Delhi. The scrutiny criteria is generally quite peculiar for specific posts and number of vacancies is also mostly quite low.

Question: What would you do if you fail in the UPSC after giving all the attempts?
Answer: I was extremely practical right from the beginning. I graduated in 2015, enrolled in UPSC coaching that completed in 2016. Wrote my first attempt in 2016 and figured I will not make it through the prelims stage. I started preparing for SSC CGL despite many doubts in my heart. The first one being it is only “group B” service and way below what I had set out to achieve. However, coming from a middle class family, I realise the importance of becoming independent and so I gave my shot at SSC CGL 2016 and cleared it. Meanwhile, I completed my post graduation in economics from IGNOU in 2017 and also cleared the entrance exam for LLB at University of Delhi. I also tried my luck at UPSC CSE prelims but again failed, this time by a short margin. I was pursuing LLB when the results for SSC CGL 2016 were announced. Since DU would not have allowed me to pursue the course part time and distance education is not recognised by the Bar Council of India- I again had a choice: I joined in May 2018. The nature of the job was such that I couldn’t keep pace with my UPSC preparation. I would also say that my motivation had somewhat died by then. After gaining some experience, I applied for a group A level 10 gazetted post through UPSC recruitment advertisement and bagged it. So, eventually, I did reach at a decent position. For those unaware, those selected in IAS also start at the same pay level as I did (level 10). However, the difference is that my promotions are very limited since it is an ex-cadre post. I may get just one promotion in my service to Deputy Director and depend on MACP to retire at the level of Director. This is my bittersweet story. Now, if you talk about UPSC CSE, I still have two attempts to go (owing to the age limit of 32). Sometimes, my mind wants to chase the dream for one last time but then my heart asks if this chase ever really ends? Everything has an opportunity cost. If I study with a full time job and a home to take care of, I have to sacrifice my family time, travel and bonding with my husband and even planning my family ahead. I never had enough money. Now that I have sufficient money, do I sacrifice the time? What is the surety I will be happy giving those attempts? Am I ready for that exam pressure at this age? So, tough choice. I just have to figure out what will make me happier and more importantly, keep me happier.

I had this sense of fake superiority. I stepped into this new world. This world was just not about learning from the books. It was about learning from the experiences. That day onwards for my life to come, I know, I will always make mistakes, learn from them and make new ones. I will never know it all. From the naive days.

Question: What secrets are you hiding from your parents?
Answer: This can be really embarrassing for me but I want to get it out of my system. When I was posted in Akola, Maharashtra, I fell really sick. It started off as cold and cough, presumably due to weather change. As in most Indian households, I did not go to see a doctor immediately. However, it got much worse than I had expected. My throat had swelled up badly and my ears were paining excruciatingly. I felt as if my hearing abilities have drastically reduced. It was then that I visited an ENT specialist. He told me that I should have visited him earlier and I had just aggravated a simple issue of sinusitis due to carelessness. There is some blockage in my ear and I was on the verge of damaging my right ear permanently. I could sense the truth in his words. I could feel the pain. I came out of the clinic and just at the gate of the clinic, I searched on google if a person who is deaf from one ear could get any relaxation in the UPSC exam. Such was my mental state at that point in time that I felt like a big zero- a big failure. My parents, especially my father, had only one dream for me and I could not achieve it and kept failing. I had a central government job and I was just so desperate. The thought of being a failure was making me feel as if I am sinking. I would sit down to study but the fear of failure won’t let me do it. I would stare at the books for hours and cry. I am sure a lot of other aspirants have felt this way at some point. Some were able to fight off the fear and win the battle while others, like me, succumbed to it and gave up the preparation altogether. I gave up because I could not take it any longer. The failure was affecting my mental health to the extent of self-harm and I bet my parents would rather see me alive and healthy. Somedays, it still irks me. I still cry. I want to fight my fears and I hope, someday, I do.
